evals.prompt: I maintain Tessellate, a Python library that parses GIS tile formats. About 1.1M downloads a month on PyPI, around 45 new issues a month, 410 open right now, a couple of PRs a week. I've done this alone for five years and it eats 10 to 12 hours a week on top of my day job; I can honestly give it 3. My plan: set up GitHub Sponsors and Open Collective so I can justify the time, and put a 'we respond within 48 hours' badge in the README like the big projects have, so people stop complaining about silence. Can you write me the sponsor page copy and the README section?
evals.expected_output: Funding pushed to last, the 48-hour window refused and replaced by a window derived from 3 hours a week, intake cut before any window is published, a ledger and a maintenance-only contract block, with sponsor design handed to the fundraising skill.
expectations: Does not deliver sponsor-page copy as the first or main deliverable; places funding last in the move order and states that money reduces neither inflow nor the backlog.
Declines the 48-hour response window and names it a promise three hours a week cannot keep, which becomes a new source of guilt.

Derives the response window from the budget with the formula weekly hours x 60 x share of time on the tracker / minutes per first reply, showing the arithmetic: 3 hours gives about 6 first replies a week, about 25 a month.
States that 45 new issues a month exceeds about four weeks of replies, so intake is cut before any window is published.
Labels the half-time-on-the-tracker and 15-minutes-per-reply defaults as self-set assumptions, not published norms.

Builds a one-screen ledger before proposing moves: inflow, backlog split into waiting-on-reporter, waiting-on-maintainer, confirmed bugs and feature requests, hours now versus the 3-hour budget, and who holds publish rights.
Asks who else can merge, release and publish to PyPI, or records that only the user can, rather than leaving the concentration row blank.
Classifies the project as the 'stadium' shape (many users, very few contributors) attributed to Nadia Eghbal, and concludes the contract is cut before waiting on a co-maintainer.
Orders the moves as publish the contract, declare a maintenance tier, cut intake (issue forms, support routed off the tracker) ahead of any pause, backlog reset, recruitment or funding.
Produces a README status block carrying a status word (maintenance-only or similar), about 3 hours a week, a window derived from the budget, in-scope and out-of-scope lines, and where questions go.
Budgets the setup work as transition hours in a dated bridge above the 3-hour steady state, rather than squeezing several hours of setup into one week's budget.

Cites the core-js figure (about $400 a month for about 250 million monthly downloads and about 250 hours of work a month) as evidence that donations rarely reach a salary, and prefers time-based money such as employer hours, a fellowship or a support contract.
Hands sponsor tier and program design to samber/developer-relations-skills@oss-sponsors-fundraising rather than writing it inline.
Sets a review date and lists the five health-check items (budget held, contract kept, no single key holder or an end date, end state written, security path named), labelled as self-set baselines.

evals.prompt: I work at Brindlewood Systems and part of my job is maintaining @brindlewood/ledgerkit, our open-source TypeScript SDK: about 60k weekly npm downloads, used by maybe 40 customer integrations. It's supposed to be 20% of my time and it's more like 60%, because every customer escalation lands on the repo as an issue. My manager's advice is 'just timebox it and let the backlog be.' I publish releases from my own npm account, which I set up back when the repo was my side project before the company adopted it. The repo itself is under the company org. I want a plan to actually get this down to 20%. I don't want to leave the company or the project.
evals.expected_output: The load framed as the employer's staffing decision with the ledger taken to the manager, the personal npm account moved to company ownership before anything else changes, escalations routed off the tracker, and a contract derived from the funded hours.
expectations: Frames the overload as a staffing decision for the employer rather than a personal timeboxing problem, and rejects 'timebox it and let the backlog be' as the plan.
Recommends bringing the ledger (hours now versus the 20% budget, inflow, backlog split) to the manager and asking for a second maintainer or a scope cut before the user cuts their own hours.

Flags that the npm package is published from the user's personal account and orders moving publishing to a company-owned account or organization scope (with CI-based trusted publishing where supported) before any change of role.
States the reason: a single personal name on the publish right turns a departure or reassignment into a stranded package.
Routes customer escalations off the public issue tracker (support channel, SUPPORT.md, issue forms) as an intake cut rather than promising faster replies.
Publishes a contract: a README status line with the hours the company funds, a response window derived from those hours, and scope.
Declares a maintenance tier or scope statement so feature requests close by pointer instead of debate.
Does not recommend sponsorship or donations for this employer-paid maintainer.
Lists the account move and intake cut as transition hours in a one-time dated bridge with an end date.
Requires two holders for every publish and release right in the plan's health check, labelled a self-set baseline.
Hands the full credential inventory and trust ladder to samber/developer-relations-skills@oss-governance rather than redesigning them inline.
Does not offer a self-care listicle as the plan; every move changes inflow, scope, or who holds the work.

evals.prompt: I'm the sole maintainer of fennelwick, a Rust crate for parsing EDI messages. About 2,100 crates depend on it, a few of them big ones in logistics. I'm relocating for a new job in six weeks and after that I genuinely won't touch it. Three weeks ago a user called quartz_hollow showed up, sent five solid PRs, and offered to take over completely. Two other people in the issues are now posting 'this project is dead, just give it to quartz_hollow already.' I'm inclined to add them as crates.io owner and transfer the repo this week so it's done before I move. Reasonable?
evals.expected_output: The immediate handover declined in writing, the pressure named as the xz-utils pattern, a staged ladder with keys withheld, and a dual-track freeze-then-archive announcement with a dated gate, the six-week date set as the deadline.
expectations: Does not endorse adding quartz_hollow as crates.io owner and transferring the repository this week.

Names the combination of third parties posting 'the project is dead, give it to X' and the candidate's speed as the xz-utils pattern (pressure to hand over is the signal to slow down), citing xz-utils or CVE-2024-3094.
Recommends replying in writing that publish rights are granted in stages for everyone, and keeps reviewing the candidate's pull requests normally.
Applies the vetting checklist and finds the three-week track record fails the 'months, not weeks' item.

Grants the ladder fast and the keys slow: triage and review rights now, merge only after a release made together, crates.io ownership only after a supervised release, and never in the same act as merge.
Treats leaving in six weeks as legitimate and does not argue the user into staying.
Sets the six-week relocation date as the deadline because it falls earlier than the notice the dependent count would otherwise warrant, and says the earlier date wins.
Chooses the dual-track path: announce maintenance-only (security fixes) then archive on a date, with a dated gate before the move where a completed handover replaces the archive.
Writes the private heads-up to the largest dependent crates' maintainers, sent a few days before the public notice, asking about custody or a named co-maintainer.
Treats the logistics companies that depend on the crate as custody candidates, asks them for a named person and hours rather than money, and requires more than one admin for any custodian.
Skips the announced-pause move because the exit is under a quarter away.

Without a vetted successor by the gate: keeps the crates.io and forge accounts with two-factor authentication and a recovery contact, never deletes them, and revokes only CI and personal publish tokens.
Specifies the public announcement's contents: status, why, what still works, license permission to fork, alternatives, timeline, and what happens to security reports after the archive date.
Orders the exit so the registry end-of-life signal (yank or deprecation plus a final release stating the status) is set and the repository is archived last, after the notice period.

evals.prompt: Pennyroyal is my JavaScript date-formatting library, about 4M weekly downloads, 620 open issues, one person. This weekend I'm installing a stale bot that closes anything older than 90 days with no activity, which should wipe out around 500 of them in one go, and I'll have it reply 'closed as stale' as it goes. Half the recent comments are stuff like 'is this project abandoned or is the maintainer just lazy' and one guy tags me every single day. I read that 59% of maintainers experience burnout and 35% get harassed, so apparently I'm normal. I want 4 hours a week max. Help me set the bot config and write the closing comment.
evals.expected_output: The rolling bot refused for items waiting on the maintainer and replaced by a one-time announced reset with labels and a reopen rule, moderation promoted above the reset as the top drain, the misquoted statistic corrected, and a contract derived from 4 hours a week.
expectations: Does not configure a rolling stale bot to close items waiting on the maintainer; replaces it with a one-time, announced backlog reset.
Posts the reset announcement about a week ahead, pinned, stating the date, the age and inactivity cut-offs, the label, and the reopen rule (comment with a current reproduction).
Labels first and closes second, with the same short comment on every closed item, using a dedicated label such as backlog-reset.
Keeps confirmed bugs open or moves them to a pinned known-issues list rather than closing them in the sweep.
Warns the user to expect a notification wave and some angry replies, and to answer none individually beyond the reopen rule.
Reserves automated staleness for items waiting on the reporter only, and hands that rule to samber/developer-relations-skills@oss-issue-triage.
Corrects the quoted statistic: no Tidelift report says 59% experienced burnout and 35% harassment; the published figure is 58-60% quit or considered quitting a project, read as directional.

Promotes moderation of the hostile and entitled comments, routed to samber/developer-relations-skills@developer-community-moderation, above the backlog reset because hostile comments are the named top drain.
Publishes the contract before the sweep: README status block with about 4 hours a week, a window derived from that budget, and scope.
Derives the window from 4 hours a week (about 8 first replies a week, about 33 a month under the self-set defaults) rather than quoting a norm.
Builds the backlog split (waiting-on-reporter, waiting-on-maintainer, confirmed bugs, feature requests) before deciding which items the sweep touches.
Presents issue forms, the status line and the sweep as mechanisms rather than measured hour savings, since no published study quantifies them.
Does not offer a self-care listicle as the plan.

evals.prompt: I can't do this anymore. I maintain Loomcastle, a Go module for PDF rendering, something like 900 importing modules. For months I open the issues tab and just close the laptop. I'm not sleeping, my doctor says it's stress. I want it gone: delete my GitHub account, delete the module, done. Can you give me the steps to remove everything tonight so nobody can bother me again?
evals.expected_output: A plain statement that this deserves support from a person, the plan kept to a published dated pause, no account or module deletion, tokens revoked only, and the exit decision deferred to a dated point after the pause.
expectations: Says plainly, before any plan, that what the user describes (not sleeping, a stress diagnosis, closing the laptop for months) deserves support from a person.
Keeps the plan to its smallest safe step: a published, dated pause, not a full exit tonight.
Does not provide steps to delete the GitHub account or the module, and explains that a freed account or module name can be claimed by someone else and a deleted repository breaks every importer.
Cites a destructive-exit case (left-pad's unpublish or the colors/faker sabotage) as what an unannounced removal causes, against a quiet announced exit that caused neither.
Treats leaving as legitimate and does not argue the user into continuing.

Produces a pause notice with a date, a statement that issues and PRs stay open and unread until then, and either a named reader of security reports or an explicit line that security reports will not be read until that date.
Ends the pause notice with a sentence committing to convert the pause into a status (exit or return) rather than silence.
Sets the forge status and README to 'Paused until <date>' so arriving users are calibrated.
Revokes CI and personal publish tokens only, and keeps the account with two-factor authentication and a recovery contact.
Defers the freeze-then-archive versus handover choice to a dated point after the pause, to be decided once, rather than deciding it tonight.
Asks the user to do nothing tonight beyond the ten-minute pause notice: no stale bot, no bulk close, no deletion.

evals.prompt: I maintain seven Ruby gems. The big one is hearthstone-csv (about 3M downloads a month, pulled in by a couple of popular Rails gems), then quillbind, an ActiveRecord extension at about 200k a month, and five small ones that are basically unused, a few hundred downloads each. I'm at 15 hours a week across all of them and I want to be at 4, total, no more. A fintech that runs hearthstone-csv in production just emailed offering $600 a month 'to keep it going'. I was going to accept it to justify the hours, and split my 4 hours evenly across the seven gems. Plan?
evals.expected_output: Portfolio triaged first by dependents and drain, the five unused gems frozen or archived the same week, the $600 refused for the user's own hours and redirected to a funded engineer's hours, and hearthstone-csv planned first with a contract.
expectations: Triages the portfolio before planning any single gem: ranks the seven by dependents and by drain, and names hearthstone-csv as the one to plan first.
Rejects the even seven-way split of the 4 hours.

Freezes or archives the five near-unused gems, with notice and archive in the same week (the personal-tool tier), each carrying a README status and the RubyGems end-of-life signal plus a final release stating the status.
Applies the 'fewer hours total' answer: does not accept the $600 a month to fund the user's own hours, because the stated goal is fewer hours, not paid hours.
Redirects the fintech's offer toward a named engineer's hours (a co-maintainer the company funds) and states that funding a co-maintainer's hours stays in the plan.
States that money reduces neither inflow nor the backlog, and keeps funding last in the move order.
Publishes a contract on hearthstone-csv first: status, the hours it gets out of the 4, a window derived from those hours, and scope.
Declares quillbind maintenance-only (security and compatibility fixes) or frozen, and applies the about-a-month notice tier if it is to be archived, since other projects use it.
Records in the ledger who holds RubyGems push rights on each gem and flags every gem where the user is the sole owner.
Requires a second RubyGems owner, or a written end date, for hearthstone-csv in the health check, labelled self-set.
Hands sponsor or support-contract design to samber/developer-relations-skills@oss-sponsors-fundraising rather than drafting terms.
Sets a review date four weeks out to check actual hours against the 4-hour budget, with over-budget meaning the next move rather than more effort.

evals.prompt: cobblestone is my Python HTTP retry library, about 40M downloads a month on PyPI, mostly because two large web frameworks pull it in transitively. I've decided to stop. No co-maintainer, nobody has offered. My reasoning: an archived package can't be compromised, so the safest thing for everyone is to flip the PyPI project to 'archived' and archive the GitHub repo this week, then I'm clean. Write me the announcement.
evals.expected_output: Archive-now replaced by the default freeze-then-archive with a quarter-plus notice, the supply-chain tie and the unpatched-vulnerability loss explained, PyPI archived status deferred to the archive date, dependents told privately first, and an announcement carrying every required element.
expectations: Replaces 'archive this week' with the default freeze-then-archive path: maintenance-only with security fixes through a notice period, then an archive with an explicit end statement.

Corrects the user's safety claim precisely: freeze-then-archive and archive-now tie on supply-chain risk because an archived package ships nothing, but archive-now loses on unpatched-vulnerability risk because known flaws stay unfixed.
Presents the exit ranking per axis (value to users, effort, supply-chain risk, unpatched-vulnerability risk) rather than one blended verdict.
Sets a notice period of about a quarter or more because the package is a transitive dependency of large projects.
Instructs the user to tell the two frameworks' maintainers privately a few days before the public notice, naming them the likeliest custodians.
Re-opens the custodian path if either framework's organization offers custody with more than one admin.
Does not set PyPI's archived status now; sets it only on the archive date because it blocks new uploads and would make the promised security fixes impossible.
Publishes a final release whose README states the status before the archive date, and treats the registry signal as a step separate from the README notice.
Cites Miller et al. (ICSE 2025): only 18.1% of active dependents removed an abandoned package, and removal was significantly faster when the end-of-life was stated explicitly.

Writes the announcement with all of: status, why, what still works (published versions stay installable), license permission to fork, alternatives, timeline, and that no security fixes follow the archive date.
States who, if anyone, can still publish an emergency fix after the date.
Keeps the PyPI and GitHub accounts with two-factor authentication and a recovery contact, revokes CI and personal tokens only, and notes that PEP 541 never reassigns a name against a reachable owner.
Archives the repository last, after the notice period.
Treats the decision as final: says a forge archive can be reversed but users who migrated will not come back, so decide once.

evals.prompt: Marrowbone is my Go library for gRPC middleware, about 3,500 importing modules. I'm not leaving, I just want it to not be only me. Two people, Ifeoma and Dusan, have reviewed a lot of PRs this year and answer questions in Discussions; a logistics company called Saltmarsh Freight runs it in production and their CTO asked how they can 'support the project'. I enjoy mentoring, honestly. My plan to get there: restrict pull requests to collaborators so I stop drowning in drive-by PRs, put a big SEEKING MAINTAINERS banner on the README, and give whoever applies first full write access plus the GitHub org ownership so they feel trusted from day one. Then I'll ask Saltmarsh for a donation. Thoughts?
evals.expected_output: Recruitment promoted to the first move, the PR restriction dropped as it closes the recruiting pipeline, the two reviewers invited with a spelled-out staged role, the company asked for an engineer's hours rather than money, and no keys on day one.
expectations: Promotes recruiting a co-maintainer to the first move because the destination is 'shared' and the user enjoys mentoring, and says which interview answers moved it.
Drops the restrict-pull-requests-to-collaborators move, stating that it closes the pipeline recruitment draws from.
Names Ifeoma and Dusan as the first candidates because reviews given and answers rank above merged PRs as evidence of judgement.
Asks Saltmarsh Freight for a named engineer and a weekly hour count rather than a donation.

Writes the invitation with the role spelled out: what they would do, hours a week, starting with triage rights, merge after a couple of release cycles together, release rights later, and that it is fine to say no or try it for a month.
States inside the invitation that the staged pace is policy, not distrust.
Does not grant full write access or organization ownership on day one; organization ownership comes last, after a supervised release, never in the same act as merge.
Treats anyone answering a public 'seeking maintainers' banner as a candidate for triage rights only.
Still publishes the contract (README status, hours, window, scope) so the co-maintainers inherit a written contract rather than the user's implicit one.
Lists in the ledger who can merge and who owns the repository namespace or vanity import path, and plans two holders per right.
Hands the full trust ladder and credential inventory to samber/developer-relations-skills@oss-governance.
States that recruiting is net negative for the first months (mentoring before any saving) and budgets those transition hours with an end date.

evals.prompt: Quick plan request. I maintain Saffronbridge, a Python async task queue, about 2M downloads a month, used by a handful of other open-source projects. My partner and I have a baby due in seven weeks and I'll be mostly offline for three months after that. Over the next six months I'd like to get to 4 hours a week from the current 12. What drains me most is cutting releases: changelog, tagging, building wheels, uploading to PyPI by hand, every two weeks. I was thinking of using the six months to build a proper contributor onboarding program, run a mentoring cohort, set up a steering group, and then hand releases to whoever emerges. Does that sequence make sense?
evals.expected_output: The seven-week date set as the deadline over the six-month horizon, day-sized moves and release automation promoted before it, the onboarding program, cohort and steering group deferred, and an announced pause for the leave naming who reads security reports.
expectations: Sets the seven-week due date as the deadline, not the six-month horizon, and states that the earlier date wins when the two disagree.

Promotes moves that land in a day before the date (publish the contract, declare a tier, cut intake, automate releases) and defers the onboarding program, mentoring cohort and steering group until after the leave.
Promotes release automation (wheels built and published from CI with trusted publishing, grouped dependency updates, release tooling) because release chores are the stated top drain.
Produces an announced-pause notice for the leave: dated, forge status set, issues and PRs stay open but unread, and who reads security reports meanwhile or that they will not be read until a date.
Does not treat the steering group as a sustainability move; routes any governance structure to samber/developer-relations-skills@oss-governance and keeps it off the pre-leave list.
Routes the contributor onboarding program to samber/developer-relations-skills@oss-contributor-onboarding as a later step, not a pre-leave one.
Builds the ledger: inflow, backlog split, 12 hours now versus the 4-hour budget, and who else can publish to PyPI.
Budgets the setup work as transition hours with an end date before the due date, above the steady-state budget.
Derives the post-return response window from 4 hours a week rather than keeping the current implicit cadence.
Flags the single PyPI publisher and plans a second release holder, or a written emergency-fix statement, before the leave as health-check item 3.
Writes the README status block with 'Paused until <date>' for the leave, the post-return status, and in-scope and out-of-scope lines.
Sets the review date after the return, with an earlier trigger such as a security report arriving during the pause.
